newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin bars constitution change, ouster bid flops.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin bars constitution change, ouster bid flops.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin rejected on Friday opposition demands for constitutional changes to water down his powers and a new attempt by his political opponents to remove him flopped.
The 66-year-old president, in his first radio address since he fell ill with pneumonia last month, rebuffed attempts to amend the constitution to reduce his powers or remove him for health reasons.
"The constitution is the pivot of the new Russian statehood," Yeltsin declared, speaking clearly but slowly in a hoarse voice.
"It is premature today to subject the new structure of the Russian state, as it is being built, to a test of its durability. It is more than that -- it is foolhardy."

The lower house of parliament later rejected a non-binding resolution suggesting Yeltsin should step down. Only 208 deputies backed the resolution proposed by a communist, 18 short of the number needed for approval.
But the chamber approved a separate motion asking Yeltsin's doctors to submit a written report on his health by March 1.
"Yeltsin effectively does not rule the state. The country is dying, in a state of deepest crisis," said Viktor Ilyukhin, who put forward the main resolution on Yeltsin's health.
Presidential press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky said the doctors would provide such a report in line with the "informational style of Kremlin openness."

Yeltsin is gradually returning to the Kremlin. He met chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais on Friday at the residence where he is recuperating outside Moscow and discussed a parliamentary address he is due to make on March 6.
Yeltsin has looked thin and moved awkwardly in television footage. One of his doctors said on Wednesday he still needed at least 10 more days to recover fully.
He has had at least two heart attacks, underwent heart surgery last November and spent 12 days in hospital with pneumonia last month.
His poor health has increased concern about the nature of the constitution, drawn up to suit his demands for a dominant role and approved in a referendum in 1993.

Proposals for constitutional changes include allowing Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin to act as president until the end of Yeltsin's scheduled term if he is unfit to govern, reducing the president's powers, setting up a state council to govern or having the next president chosen by parliament.

Yeltsin set aside the old constitution in September 1993 by exceeding his authority and dissolving the sitting parliament. When opponents launched an armed uprising from the legislature's headquarters, he used troops to crush resistance.
The armed forces which so hesitantly backed Yeltsin then now face crisis. A non-government research organisation said the army faced a collapse that could lead to civil war or a military coup.
"The army has long ceased to be a guarantee against external threats," said a statement by the Council for Foreign and Defence Policy, published in the daily Nezavisimaya Gazeta.
